requirement:
When authoring evidence for a named example, its complete fenced declaration
MUST be included in the mandatory input set defined by
{cite}`requirements.authoring.mandatory_inputs`.
rationale:
**Verdict:** the requirement is met. The one weakness is a test assertion that is weaker than it could be.

**Requirement:** when authoring an example, its complete fenced declaration must be in the mandatory input set from `requirements.authoring.mandatory_inputs`.

**Implementation** (`AssessmentSources::prepare`, `src/authoring/inputs.rs`, marked `{impl}` for `requirements.examples.authoring_inputs`):
- `prepare` accepts any non-term definition, so named examples are valid subjects. Its first selector is always `InputSelector::Requirements { requirements: subject_name }`.
- `source_input` and `InputSelector::resolve` (`src/inputs.rs`) turn that selector into text taken from the declaration's `raw_lines`.
- `raw_lines` is built in `src/evidence.rs` (around line 397). It holds the whole block from the opening `:::{example} name` fence to the closing `:::`. Only `:impl:`/`:test:` option lines are stripped, which is consistent with how the project treats those lines as not part of the declaration text.
- `src/evidence.rs` (around line 2162) has a unit test asserting that `raw_lines` is `[":::{req} ready", "Ready MUST hold.", ":::"]`. Requirements and examples go through the same extraction path.
- `generated_evidence_selector` never drops a `Requirements` selector. The subject declaration therefore can't be filtered out as generated evidence, and `prepare` pushes it into `mandatory` in its original position.
- `prepare` also adds cited declarations, `{impl}`/`{test}` sources and terminology. These are covered by other requirements that `prepare` also marks.
- The implementation marking is complete. `prepare`, `source_input` and `resolve` carry the relevant `{impl}` markers, and I found no unmarked code that implements this obligation.

**Test** (`bundle_combines_direct_references_terms_and_current_existing_selectors`, marked `{test}` for this requirement):
- The test builds a project with a named example, `requirements.case`.
- It calls `AssessmentSources::prepare(root, "requirements.case")`.
- It asserts that `subject_kind` is `Definition(DefinitionKind::Example)`.
- It asserts that `mandatory_inputs()[0]["requirements"] == "requirements.case"`.
- So the test proves that an example subject yields a declaration input for itself.

**Gap:** the test does not assert that the input text includes the opening and closing fences. That property is covered indirectly by the shared `raw_lines` unit test in `src/evidence.rs` and by the single code path for all definitions. I judged it too small to fail the requirement.

Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. `{impl}` and `{test}` point from the definition to the source, so the source becomes a mandatory input to the definition's assessment, and that definition's evidence must cover the reference line. `{cite}` points from the source to the definition: a citing requirement or example receives the cited declaration as context, and the citing site needs no evidence coverage. Marking only `{cite}` on code that implements part of a requirement leaves a gap in that requirement's review. In the book, references and definitions become linked badges.

Some sources cannot or should not carry a reference themselves, such as a shipped agent skill. A requirement can anchor such a file with `:impl:` or `:test:` option lines immediately after its opening fence; an example can use `:test:`. Each anchor is an edge to the complete file, so that requirement's evidence must contain an input covering every line of it, and changing the file makes the evidence stale. Option lines are not part of the requirement text. Prefer a precise in-source reference whenever one is possible.
